title: Shell basics & getting help
about: What a shell is and how it runs a line, builtin vs external commands, PATH, exit statuses, command separators, line editing, and finding help with man, info and less.

questions.title: Role of the shell
questions.text: Which statement best describes what a shell such as `bash` does?
questions.note: The kernel, the shell and the terminal window are three different things: the shell is a normal program that talks to the kernel for you.

options.t: It is a program that reads text commands, interprets them and starts other programs on your behalf, and it also offers a small programming language.
options.why: That is the whole job: a text interface between you and the operating system, plus scripting (variables, `if`, loops) on top.

options.t: It is the part of the kernel that schedules processes and manages memory.
options.why: That is the kernel itself. The shell is an ordinary user-space program; it asks the kernel to do things through system calls.

options.t: It is the graphical desktop that draws windows and menus.
options.why: A desktop environment does that. A terminal emulator window merely *hosts* a shell; the shell has nothing to do with drawing windows.

options.t: It is a compiler that turns a script into a binary executable before running it.
options.why: Shell scripts are interpreted line by line. Nothing is compiled ahead of time.

questions.title: Shell versus terminal
questions.text: What is the relationship between a terminal emulator (e.g. `xterm`, GNOME Terminal) and the shell running inside it?

options.t: The terminal emulator only provides the window, keyboard input and text output; the shell is a separate program started inside it.
options.why: Correct. You can run `zsh` or `dash` inside the same emulator and nothing about the window changes.

options.t: They are the same program, so changing the terminal changes the shell.
options.why: They are separate. Changing the emulator leaves your shell (and its settings) as it was.

options.t: The terminal emulator interprets the commands and the shell only draws the text.
options.why: Reversed. The shell parses and runs commands; the emulator only displays characters and forwards keystrokes.

options.t: The shell runs only in a terminal emulator; over SSH or on a text console there is no shell.
options.why: A shell is what you get on a text console (tty) and over SSH too; no graphical emulator is required.

questions.title: Shells in the Unix family
questions.text: Select every program that is a command interpreter (shell) on Unix-like systems.

options.why: The Bourne-Again Shell, the default on most Linux distributions.
The Korn shell, another classic Bourne-style shell.
A C-shell derivative, with a different syntax from bash.
A terminal emulator: it draws a window and runs a shell in it, but it is not an interpreter itself.
A pager for reading text one screen at a time.

questions.title: Default prompt symbol
questions.text: For an ordinary user bash normally ends the prompt with `{{0}}`; for root it ends with `{{1}}`.
questions.note: The `#` for root is a visual warning that you are running with unlimited privileges.

wrong.why: `>` is the *continuation* prompt (PS2) shown when a command is unfinished, not the normal prompt.

questions.title: What the shell does with each line
questions.text: Put the steps of the shell's interactive cycle in order.

items.why: The shell announces it is ready for a command.

items.t: Read a line typed by the user
items.why: It cannot analyse anything until the line exists.

items.t: Analyse the line (split it into words, expand, find redirections)
items.why: Parsing and expansion must happen before anything can be launched.

items.t: Run the command(s) and normally wait for them to finish
items.why: Only after the line is understood can the program be started; in the foreground the shell waits.

items.t: Go back to printing the prompt
items.why: The loop repeats until the shell exits.

questions.title: Several commands on one line
questions.text: What does `echo one; echo two` print?

options.t: `one` and `two` on two separate lines, the second command running after the first finishes.
options.why: `;` separates commands, which are run one after the other.

options.t: `one; echo two` on one line, because everything after `echo` is its argument.
options.why: Unquoted `;` is shell syntax, not text, so the line is split into two commands.

options.t: A syntax error, because each line may hold only one command.
options.why: Several commands per line are allowed; `;` is exactly the separator for that.

options.t: `two` only, because the last command overwrites the first output.
options.why: Output is written to the terminal, not stored; nothing is overwritten.

questions.title: Quoting a semicolon
questions.text: What is the output of `echo I love bash ";" really`?

options.why: Quotes make `;` ordinary text, so it is passed to `echo` as an argument.

options.t: `I love bash`, followed by the error `really: command not found`
options.why: That would happen without the quotes; inside quotes `;` no longer ends the command.
`echo` prints every argument it gets, including `;`. The quotes only stop the shell from interpreting it.
A quoted `;` is just a character; there is nothing for the parser to complain about.

questions.title: Builtin versus external
questions.text: What is the defining difference between a builtin and an external command?

options.t: A builtin is implemented inside the shell itself, while an external command is a separate executable file the shell must find and start.
options.why: Correct: a builtin runs as a shell function; an external command needs a new process and a file on disk.

options.t: A builtin is always faster to type, an external one needs a full path.
options.why: Typing has nothing to do with it; external commands are found through `PATH` without a full path.

options.t: A builtin can only be used in scripts, an external one only interactively.
options.why: Both kinds work in either place.

options.t: A builtin runs as root, an external command runs as the current user.
options.why: Privileges come from the user who started the shell, not from the command type.

questions.title: Builtin or external
questions.text: Classify each command as it is typically found in bash on Linux.

items.why: It must change the working directory of the shell process itself, so it cannot be a separate program.
It lists the jobs of the current shell, information only the shell has.
It resumes one of the shell's jobs; a child process could not do that.
A separate program that asks the kernel to create a directory.

questions.title: Why cd is a builtin
questions.text: Why can `cd` not work as a normal external program?

options.t: The working directory belongs to each process, so an external program would change only its own directory and die, leaving the shell where it was.
options.why: A child process cannot alter its parent's working directory, so the command has to run inside the shell.

options.t: Because `cd` needs root privileges to read other directories.
options.why: It needs no extra privilege; access follows normal directory permissions.

options.t: Because there is no disk space for a `cd` binary in `/bin`.
options.why: Size is irrelevant. The reason is process isolation.

options.t: Because `cd` is a keyword of the C language.
options.why: Coincidence of name only; it has no connection to C.

questions.title: Identifying a command
questions.text: Which commands can tell you whether `ls` is a builtin, an alias or a file, and where that file is?

options.why: A bash builtin that reports how the name would be interpreted (alias, builtin, keyword or file).
Searches the `PATH` and prints the first executable found, though it does not know about builtins or aliases.
Looks for the binary, its manual page and sources in standard locations.
Prints only the one-line manual description; it says nothing about where the command lives.
Searches the descriptions of manual pages for a keyword.

questions.title: What type reveals
questions.text: Running `type cd` in bash prints `cd is a shell builtin`. What would `type ls` most likely print on a typical system?

options.t: `ls is /usr/bin/ls` (or an alias description if an alias exists)
options.why: `ls` is an external file found through `PATH`.
`ls` is not implemented inside bash.
`ls` exists on every Linux system.
Keywords are words such as `if`, `for`, `while`; `ls` is a normal command.

questions.title: Builtin also on disk
questions.text: `type -a echo` on a typical Linux system lists both `echo is a shell builtin` and `echo is /usr/bin/echo`. What happens when you type `echo hi`?

options.t: The builtin runs, because bash looks for builtins before searching `PATH`.
options.why: Builtins take precedence over same-named files.

options.t: The file `/usr/bin/echo` runs, because files are always preferred.
options.why: The opposite is true.

options.t: Bash asks you which one you mean.
options.why: Bash never asks; the lookup order is fixed.

options.t: Both run and the text is printed twice.
options.why: Only the first match in the lookup order is used.

questions.title: Lookup of a command name
questions.text: When you type a command name without a slash, bash finds an external program by searching the directories listed in the variable `{{0}}`.
questions.note: `PATH` is a colon-separated list of directories, searched from left to right; the first match wins.

wrong.why: `HOME` is your home directory, not a list of program directories.

questions.title: Running a program outside PATH
questions.text: You wrote a script `tool.sh` in your current directory, and `.` is not in `PATH`. Which command runs it (assuming it is executable)?

options.why: A name containing a slash is used as a path, so no `PATH` search happens.
With no slash the shell searches only `PATH`, does not find it and reports `command not found`.
There is no such standard command.
That expands a variable called `tool` followed by `.sh`; it does not run a file.

questions.title: Command not found
questions.text: You type `mytool` and get `command not found`, yet `ls -l ./mytool` shows an executable file. What is the most likely cause?

options.t: The directory that contains it is not in `PATH`, so the bare name is never searched there.
options.why: Exactly. Use `./mytool` or add the directory to `PATH`.

options.t: The file needs `sudo` to be seen by the shell.
options.why: Missing permissions produce `Permission denied`, not `command not found`.

options.t: `ls` has a different `PATH` from the shell.
options.why: `ls` does not search anything; you gave it a path.

options.t: Executable files only run after a reboot.
options.why: There is no such rule.

questions.title: Looking up a command word
questions.text: Order these steps of how bash resolves the first word of a simple command, from first to last.

items.t: Expand an alias if one matches
items.why: Aliases are rewritten first, before anything else is decided.

items.t: Check for a shell function of that name
items.why: Functions are the shell's own definitions and win over programs on disk.

items.t: Check for a builtin of that name
items.why: Builtins are built into bash and are tried before disk lookups.

items.t: Search the directories of `PATH` for an executable file
items.why: This disk search is the last resort.

questions.title: Meaning of exit status
questions.text: What does a command's exit status of `0` mean?

options.why: By convention 0 is success, and any other number signals some kind of failure.
A command can do a lot and still return 0.
A killed process gets a status above 128 (128 plus the signal number).

options.t: The command ran in the background.
options.why: Background execution is a different matter and has no special status.

questions.title: Reading the status
questions.text: Which variable holds the exit status of the last command?

options.why: Holds the status of the most recently finished foreground command.
Holds the process ID of the current shell.
Holds the PID of the last background process.
Holds the number of arguments of a script or function.

questions.title: Common exit statuses
questions.text: Match each situation with the exit status bash reports.

pairs.why: GNU `ls` uses 2 for a serious problem such as a missing path.

pairs.l: The command word is not found anywhere
pairs.why: Bash's special code for `command not found`.

pairs.l: The file exists but is not executable
pairs.why: Bash's code for "found but cannot be executed".

extras.why: Not assigned to any of these situations; a suspended process has not even exited, so it has no status yet.

questions.title: Status after echo
questions.text: After `false; echo $?` you see `1`. In the line `echo hello; echo $?`, what does the second `echo` print?

options.t: `0`, the status of the first `echo`, which succeeded.
options.why: `$?` always refers to the previous command, here the first `echo`.
Every command that finishes overwrites the stored status.
`$?` is a number, not the command's output.

options.t: Nothing, `$?` is empty until a script ends.
options.why: It is set after every command, including at the prompt.

questions.title: Status-based separators
questions.text: Select the statements that are true about `&&` and `||`.

options.why: `&&` means "and then, if it worked".
`||` means "otherwise".

options.t: `a; b` runs `b` regardless of how `a` ended.
options.why: The plain semicolon ignores the status.
That is the behaviour of `||`.
`b` is skipped when `a` succeeds.

questions.title: Evaluate a chain
questions.text: What is printed by `false && echo A || echo B`?

options.why: `false` fails, so `&& echo A` is skipped; the `||` sees a failure and runs `echo B`.
`A` would need `false` to succeed.
`A` is never run.
The `||` branch runs because the left side did not succeed.

questions.title: Success then fail
questions.text: What does `true && false || echo X` print?

options.why: `true && false` ends with status 1, so the `||` branch runs.
The chain is evaluated left to right; the status that reaches `||` is the one of `false`.
Builtins `true` and `false` print nothing; they only set the status.
Mixing `&&` and `||` is legal.

questions.title: Test a file then act
questions.text: Complete the line so that `make` runs only if `cd build` succeeded: `cd build {{0}} make`
questions.note: `&&` is the safe way to chain steps that depend on each other.

wrong.why: With `;` make would run even when `cd build` failed, in the wrong directory.
That would run `make` only when `cd build` failed, exactly the opposite of the goal.

groups.title: Getting help: man, whatis, apropos, info

questions.title: The manual sections
questions.text: Which number is the manual section for commands available to ordinary users (like `ls`)?

options.why: Section 1 holds user commands.
Section 2 documents system calls of the kernel.
Section 5 describes file formats such as `passwd`.
Section 8 is for system administration commands run by root.

questions.title: Manual sections
questions.text: Match each section with its content.

extras.why: The manual has no section for tutorials; it documents commands, calls and formats.

questions.title: Choosing a section
questions.text: `write` exists as a command and as a system call. Which command opens the page of the **system call**?

options.why: The section number goes before the name; 2 is system calls.
Bash passes `2` as a second page name, not a section.
There is no such option.
Without a section, man shows the first match, which is the user command in section 1.

questions.title: Search by keyword
questions.text: You do not know the name of the command that compresses files but remember the word "compress". Which command searches the manual descriptions for it?

options.why: It searches names and short descriptions for the keyword.
It looks for pages whose *name* is exactly `compress`, so you must already know the name.
It locates binaries and pages of a known command.
It only shows the path of an executable that already exists.

questions.title: Equivalent ways to search manuals
questions.text: Select the commands that search manual-page descriptions for a keyword.

options.why: Keyword search of names and descriptions.
`-k` makes `man` behave like `apropos`.
Matches only pages whose name is `directory`.
Opens the info document called `directory`; it is not a search.

questions.title: What whatis prints
questions.text: What does `whatis ls` print?

options.t: The one-line description of each manual page named `ls`.
options.why: `whatis` is a quick lookup of short descriptions by exact name.
That is `man ls`.
That is `which ls`.

options.t: Every page that mentions the word `ls`.
options.why: That would be `apropos ls`.

questions.title: Open a manual page
questions.text: To read the manual page of the command `sort`, type: `{{0}} sort`
questions.note: `man name` opens the page in a pager (normally `less`).

wrong.why: `help` documents bash *builtins*. `sort` is an external program, so there is no help entry.
It prints only a one-line summary, not the page.

questions.title: Leaving man
questions.text: Which key quits a manual page displayed by `man`?

options.why: `man` uses a pager (`less`), where `q` means quit.
Not used by `less`.
Esc alone does nothing in `less`.
That is the vi editor, not a pager.

questions.title: What info adds
questions.text: How do GNU `info` documents differ from manual pages?

options.t: They are organised as a tree of linked nodes with menus and cross-references, instead of one long linear page.
options.why: That hypertext structure is the main difference.

options.t: They are shorter summaries of man pages.
options.why: They are often longer and more detailed.

options.t: They can be edited by users and saved.
options.why: They are read-only documentation.

options.t: They can only be read in a graphical environment.
options.why: The standard `info` reader runs in a terminal.

questions.title: Navigating info
questions.text: Match each key in the `info` reader with its action.

pairs.r: Next node on the same level
pairs.why: Moves forward in the sequence of sibling nodes.

pairs.r: Previous node on the same level
Up one level in the tree
Go back to the last node you visited

extras.why: No such action exists; info documents are read-only.

questions.title: Menu entries in info
questions.text: In an `info` page, how do you follow a link shown as `* Common options::`?

options.t: Move the cursor onto it and press Enter.
options.why: Enter jumps to the node behind the menu entry or cross-reference.
That sends an interrupt and does not follow links.
`man` knows nothing about info nodes.

options.t: Links cannot be followed; info pages are plain text.
options.why: Following links is exactly what makes info hypertext.

questions.title: Why less
questions.text: Why does `man` show pages through `less` instead of just printing them?

options.t: `less` shows one screen at a time and lets you scroll and search, without loading the whole file first.
options.why: A pager makes long text readable.

options.t: `less` translates the page into your language.
options.why: It only displays text.
Protection comes from file permissions, not the pager.

options.t: Because the terminal cannot print more than 24 lines.
options.why: Terminals can scroll; the pager is for convenience.

questions.title: Keys in less
questions.text: Match each key in `less` with what it does.

pairs.why: Go to the start of the text.
Go to the end of the text.
Next match in the same direction.

questions.title: Searching in a manual
questions.text: Inside a man page, typing `{{0}}error` starts a forward search for the word error, and pressing `{{1}}` jumps to the next match.
questions.note: `/` searches forward, `?` searches backward, `n` repeats, `N` repeats in the opposite direction.

questions.title: less versus more
questions.text: Compared with the older `more`, what is an advantage of `less`?

options.t: You can scroll backwards as well as forwards, and search in both directions.
options.why: That flexibility gave `less` its name, as a joke on "less is more".

options.t: It can edit the file while viewing it.
options.why: Neither is an editor.

options.t: It is the only pager that works with pipes.
options.why: Both can read from a pipe.
Sorting is `sort`'s job.

questions.title: Bash line-editing keys
questions.text: Select the keys that work at the bash prompt as described.

options.t: `Tab` completes a command or file name.
options.why: Completion saves typing and avoids typos.

options.t: `↑` recalls the previous command from history.
options.why: Repeated presses walk further back.

options.t: `Ctrl+A` moves the cursor to the start of the line.
options.why: Emacs-style editing keys are the default in bash.

options.t: `Ctrl+E` moves the cursor to the end of the line.
options.why: The counterpart of `Ctrl+A`.
`Ctrl+Z` suspends the running command; it edits nothing.

questions.title: Reverse search
questions.text: What does `Ctrl+R` do at the bash prompt?

options.t: It starts an incremental search backwards through your command history.
options.why: Type a few letters and the most recent matching command appears; press it again for older ones.

options.t: It repeats the last command immediately.
options.why: Repeating the last command is `!!`.
Reloading is `source ~/.bashrc`.

options.t: It removes the last command from history.
options.why: `Ctrl+R` only searches.

questions.title: Keys that talk to the running program
questions.text: Match each key with its effect.

pairs.why: It sends `SIGINT` to the foreground job.
It sends `SIGTSTP`; the job is stopped, not killed.
At an empty prompt it also ends the shell.
The same effect as the `clear` command.

extras.why: That is `Ctrl+W`. None of the keys above does it.

questions.title: History expansion
questions.text: After running `ls /etc`, what does typing `!!` and Enter do?

options.why: `!!` expands to the last command line.
That is the `history` command.
Commands already finished cannot be cancelled.

options.t: It negates the previous command's exit status.
options.why: A single `!` does that at command start; `!!` is history.

questions.title: Anatomy of a command
questions.text: In `ls -l /etc`, what are `-l` and `/etc`?

options.t: Two arguments passed to the command `ls`: an option and an operand.
options.why: The shell splits the line into words; the first is the command, the rest are its arguments.
Only the first word is the command.
Variables are set with `NAME=value`.
Comments start with `#`.

questions.title: Whitespace splitting
questions.text: How many arguments does `echo a    b` (four spaces between) pass to `echo`, and what does it print?

options.t: Two arguments, `a` and `b`; it prints `a b` with a single space.
options.why: The shell splits on runs of blanks, and `echo` joins arguments with one space.
That needs quoting: `echo "a    b"`.
Blanks are separators, not arguments.

options.t: It fails because of the extra spaces.
options.why: Extra blanks are simply ignored.

questions.title: Double quotes keep spacing
questions.text: What does `echo "a    b"` print?

options.t: `a    b` with the four spaces intact.
options.why: Quotes stop word splitting, so `echo` receives a single argument.
That is the unquoted result.
The shell removes the quotes before `echo` sees the argument.
Quoting is perfectly valid.

questions.title: Comments
questions.text: Everything after a `{{0}}` character that starts a word is a comment and is ignored by bash.
questions.note: In scripts a `#` at the start of a word begins a comment; a `#` inside a word, such as `a#b`, is ordinary text.

wrong.why: `//` is a comment in C-like languages, but in bash it is just text.
`--` is used to end options, it is not a comment.

questions.title: First word of a command
questions.text: In `FOO=bar env | grep FOO`, how does the shell treat `FOO=bar`?

options.t: As a variable assignment placed in the environment of the `env` command only.
options.why: Assignments before a command name are temporary and apply just to that command.

options.t: As the name of the command to run.
options.why: A leading `NAME=value` is recognised as an assignment, not as a command.

options.t: As an error because assignments must be on their own line.
options.why: Prefix assignments are legal.

options.t: As a permanent change of your shell's environment.
options.why: The setting disappears after the command ends.

groups.title: Sessions and the prompt in practice

questions.title: Exiting the shell
questions.text: Which way ends an interactive bash session?

options.t: Typing `exit`, or pressing `Ctrl+D` at an empty prompt.
options.why: Both end the shell; `Ctrl+D` sends end-of-input.
That just gives a new prompt.
That suspends the foreground job; at an empty prompt it does nothing useful.
Bash has no `quit` command.

questions.title: Long commands over several lines
questions.text: What does a backslash at the very end of a line do in bash?

options.t: It escapes the newline, so the command continues on the next line.
options.why: Handy for splitting long commands for readability.

options.t: It ends the command with an error.
options.why: A trailing backslash is valid.
The backslash-newline pair is removed before execution.

options.t: It runs the command in the background.
options.why: That is the job of `&`.

questions.title: Which shell am I in
questions.text: Which command shows the name of the shell program you are currently running (in a typical bash session)?

options.why: `$0` expands to the name of the running shell (for example `bash`).
`$#` is the number of arguments, not a program name.
That prints the last exit status.
That prints your home directory.

questions.title: Exit status in prompts
questions.text: Why do many people show the last exit status in their prompt?

options.t: To notice immediately when the previous command failed, without typing `echo $?`.
options.why: Useful feedback when you chain many commands.

options.t: Because bash refuses to run a command after a failed one.
options.why: Bash does not block anything; every command runs regardless.

options.t: Because the status decides who owns the next file.
options.why: Ownership is unrelated to exit status.

options.t: Because it is required by POSIX.
options.why: No standard requires it; it is a convenience.

questions.title: Unquoted semicolon surprise
questions.text: What happens when you run `echo a;b` (no spaces, nothing quoted)?

options.t: `a` is printed, then bash reports that `b` is not found as a command.
options.why: The `;` splits the line into `echo a` and `b`; `b` is then searched as a command name.
That would need quotes: `echo "a;b"`.

options.t: `a` and `b` are printed on separate lines.
options.why: `b` is a command, not text to print, so it is looked up in `PATH`.

options.t: Bash reports a syntax error and runs nothing.
options.why: The line is syntactically valid; the failure happens at run time for `b`.

questions.title: Status after a failed cd
questions.text: In a directory where `cd /nonexistent` fails, what does `echo $?` print right after it?

options.why: `cd` failed, and failure is any non-zero status.
Printing an error message does not make a command succeed.

options.t: The name of the current directory.
options.why: `$?` only holds a number.

options.t: Nothing, because failed builtins do not set `$?`.
options.why: Every command, builtin or not, sets it.

questions.title: Status of a subshell
questions.text: What does `bash -c "exit 3"; echo $?` print?

options.why: The child shell ended with `exit 3`, and the parent stored that number in `$?`.

options.t: `0` because the parent shell itself did not fail.
options.why: `$?` reports the child command that just finished, not the parent.
`$?` is a number, never the command text.
`bash -c` runs a command string as a tiny script, so `exit` works.

questions.title: Ways to get help on a command
questions.text: Select the ways that show documentation for the `grep` command on a typical Linux system.

options.why: Opens the manual page.
Most GNU programs print a short usage summary with `--help`.
Opens the info manual, if installed.
Shows how the name is resolved (for example its path), not documentation.
Prints the path of the executable only.

questions.title: Help for a builtin
questions.text: `cd` is a bash builtin and has no separate program. Which command prints its built-in help text?

options.why: `help` is a bash builtin that documents the shell's own builtins.
That would search for the text `cd` in standard input.
It looks for files; a builtin has none.
`cd` treats that as a directory name and fails.

questions.title: What whereis reports
questions.text: Which pieces of information can `whereis ls` print?

options.why: It searches the standard binary directories.

options.t: The location of the manual page for `ls`.
options.why: It also looks in the manual directories.

options.t: The exit status of the last run of `ls`.
options.why: It knows nothing about earlier executions.

options.t: The list of files in the current directory.
options.why: That is what running `ls` itself does.

questions.title: Cancel a half-typed line
questions.text: You typed part of a command and change your mind. Which key combination abandons the line and gives you a fresh prompt?

options.why: At the prompt it discards what you typed and starts a new line.
It suspends running programs; at the prompt it does not clear the line.
On a non-empty line it does nothing useful (and on an empty one it exits).
It clears the screen but keeps the line you typed.

questions.title: If tests the status
questions.text: What does `if grep -q root /etc/passwd; then echo yes; fi` check?

options.t: Whether `grep` exits with status 0, meaning that it found a match.
options.why: `if` runs the command and branches on its exit status.

options.t: Whether the text `root` is printed on the screen.
options.why: With `-q` grep prints nothing; only the status matters.
Only indirectly: if it cannot be read, grep fails.
No variable is involved.

questions.title: Order of evaluation
questions.text: Which lines does `true || echo X; false || echo Y; true && echo Z` print?

options.why: `X` is skipped because `true` succeeded; `false` fails so `Y` runs; `true` succeeds so `Z` runs.
`||` does not run its right side after a success.
`X` would need the left side to fail.
Two of the three right-hand sides do run.

questions.title: Path versus name
questions.text: `/bin/ls` and `ls` run the same program on most systems. What is the difference in how bash finds it?

options.t: With a slash in the word bash uses that path directly; without one it searches `PATH` (after aliases, functions and builtins).
options.why: A word containing `/` bypasses the lookup order entirely.

options.t: `/bin/ls` is slower because it needs root.
options.why: No privilege is needed to run it by its path.

options.t: There is no difference at all, bash always searches `PATH`.
options.why: A word with a slash is never searched in `PATH`.

options.t: `ls` runs the builtin version and `/bin/ls` the external one.
options.why: `ls` is not a builtin in bash.
